title: Each held a part
hook: the blind men and the elephant, read whole

segments.voice: Yesterday: Meghiya in the mango grove, and your line, not yet ripe. Did you let one piece of advice be heard? Today, a story you already know, read again from its home in the Udana. Day six hundred nineteen.

Near the start of this year, on day three hundred fifty-eight, you heard the blind men and the elephant: water pot, winnowing basket, plowshare, broom. It's one of the most retold stories in the world, on posters and in classrooms and in other traditions too. But most retellings keep only the middle. They drop how it starts and how it ends. Today we're reading it whole, from its place in the sixth chapter of the Udana, and paying attention to three things the short version leaves out: who it was told to, the line about the king, and the verse. Today: each held a part.
screen: `WATER POT, BASKET, PLOWSHARE, BROOM.` → `MOST RETELLINGS KEEP THE MIDDLE.` → `TODAY, THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. The monks come back from town troubled. Teachers of many groups are arguing: is the world eternal or not, finite or not, is the soul the same as the body, does one who is awakened exist after death. And they're wounding each other, the text says, with mouths like daggers. So the story is told to the monks, about a city full of argument. Second, the king. After the blind men fight with their fists, the text says simply that the king was delighted. Why? The text doesn't explain. Some readers hear him as a man enjoying a spectacle he arranged; others hear the delight of someone who sees the whole while the others see parts. The text leaves it open, and so will we. And notice something easy to miss: none of the men lied. The one at the ear really did feel a winnowing basket. Each report was true about its part. What went wrong was the word only. Third, the verse, which the Buddha speaks after telling the story. Some teachers and seekers, it says, are attached to these views. They quarrel and dispute, people who see just one side. Look at the shape of it. The problem isn't seeing a part; everyone sees a part. The problem is clinging, and then fighting. Last time the lesson was hear out a view you dislike. Today it goes further: listen to the whole, before you judge.
screen: `MOUTHS LIKE DAGGERS.` · `THE KING WAS DELIGHTED.` · `NO ONE LIED; THE WORD WAS ONLY.` · `PEOPLE WHO SEE ONE SIDE.` · then, large: `EACH HELD A PART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen fully before judging. Sit and settle. Bring to mind a recent moment when you made up your mind about someone before they'd finished talking. Replay it slowly. What part were they holding? What part were you holding? Is there a word only hiding in your own view? Don't argue it out. Just let both parts sit side by side, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Each held a part. In Udana 6.4, every blind man's report was true about his part; the quarrel came from clinging to one side. Today's word.
Your line: each held a part. Today, in one conversation, wait until the other person has completely finished before you decide anything. Day six hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the elephant story when teaching about clinging to views, and versions of it are also told in Jain, Hindu and Sufi traditions, each with its own lesson.

fork.setup: you're one of the men who touched the elephant's ear. you're sure it's like a winnowing basket. another man insists it's like a post. what does the verse warn against?
options: clinging to your side and fighting over it.
fork.reveal: everyone touches a part. the verse names those who cling to one side and quarrel as the ones who go wrong.

original.note: Pali ditthi: a view, an opinion. in Udana 6.4 the teachers cling to their ditthi.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story says everyone is a little bit right.
what it means: each report was true about its part; the fault was clinging to one side and fighting over it.
what a scholar hears: Udana 6.4 lists the ten undeclared questions as the teachers' disputes, and is followed by two more suttas (6.5, 6.6) with the same frame.
